Abstract:
The dissolution of Mn and Fe in liquid Al presents a challenge due to their high melting points and low diffusivity. A literature review reveals that the existing knowledge of the processes involved in the dissolution of both Fe and Mn in liquid Al is rather ambiguous. Thus, this work aimed to obtain more detailed insights into the dissolution behavior of Mn and Fe in various Al melts. The results of the Mn dissolution tests showed that three intermediate phases were involved in the dissolution process, all of which exhibited a smooth interface between Mn and the liquid. These three phases were identified as the γ2, Al11Mn4, and µ phases which grow slowly, penetrating the Mn particles. The results of the Fe dissolution tests showed that in pure Al, the Al5Fe2 phase dominates the dissolution process and penetrates the Fe particles. The addition of Ti into the molten Al alters the intermetallic compound formation by replacing Al5Fe2 by Al2Fe. The addition of Si significantly inhibited the Fe dissolution kinetics. A theoretical approach based on Ficks’ law was used to explain the experimentally obtained Mn and Fe dissolution rates. It showed that the surface area and shape of the additives significantly affected the dissolution processes.

The excerpt describes dissolution as mass-transfer controlled and models the Mn and Fe flux through a liquid diffusion boundary layer using Fick’s law. After 9 minutes, the calculated fluxes into a 500 g aluminum melt are 3.2 × 10^-3 g/s for Mn and 9.2 × 10^-3 g/s for Fe. Thus, the measured Fe dissolution flux is about 2.9 times the Mn flux, although a simplified calculation based on comparable convection and phase-layer thickness predicts Fe to be 1.4 times higher. The discrepancy is attributed partly to Fe flakes disintegrating into smaller particles and therefore having greater reactive surface area, while compact as-cast Mn flakes mainly react at their surface. The Mn dissolution rate constant is approximately 1.5 × 10^-5 m/s, and stronger stirring increases dissolution: 5-second stirring produced a substantially higher Mn rate than 3-second stirring. Dissolution was studied at approximately 750 °C; the excerpt specifically reports concentrations and microstructures after 9 minutes, rather than a definitive time required for complete dissolution. Dissolution proceeds through intermediate intermetallic phases rather than direct solid dissolution. In the Al-Mn system, Al11Mn4, a lambda-designated phase, and c2 were observed, with Al11Mn4 and lambda having similar thicknesses and c2 somewhat thinner. The excerpt does not identify the Fe intermetallic phases.

The c2 layer is relatively thin and is identified as the principal obstacle to Al diffusion; void formation near the c2/Mn interface indicates a Kirkendall effect, which progressively reduces bonding and inhibits further dissolution. ## pqac-00000019

From text 'shapiro2007brazingoftitanium pages 11-14'.

AE Shapiro and YA Flom. Brazing of titanium at temperatures below 800^ oc: review and prospective applications. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt does not provide a quantitative dissolution rate or a complete kinetic law for solid titanium dissolving in molten aluminum. It indicates that interaction is strongly temperature- and time-dependent. Wetting improves substantially as temperature rises: contact angles for several commercial aluminum alloys decrease from about 70° at 670°C to 20–30° at 740°C, while brazing experiments commonly use approximately 670–720°C. Intermetallic growth increases with brazing temperature; joints brazed at 710–720°C were weaker than those brazed at 670–680°C. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72256-4, doi:10.1038/s41467-026-72256-4. This article has 0 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies 12.7 wt.% Er as the Al-Er eutectic composition and discusses Al-10Er (wt.%) as a representative near-eutectic alloy for LPBF processing. It also gives the Al-Sc eutectic composition as 0.5 wt.% Sc and cites the Al-Ce eutectic composition as 9.3 wt.% Ce. No specific Zr or Mn compositions are provided in the excerpt, and no experimentally established optimum Er content is explicitly stated. The text explains that near-eutectic compositions are selected to create a continuous eutectic nano-skeleton, while the Al-Er system is favored because Al3Er is deformable, crystallographically compatible with α-Al, and capable of contributing to grain refinement and precipitation strengthening. Thus, the excerpt supports 10 wt.% Er as a representative investigated composition and 12.7 wt.% Er as the thermodynamic eutectic composition, but it does not by itself establish that either value is the optimum Er content for LPBF.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'li2026strong3dprintedaluminium pages 10-16'.

Yang Li, Tingting Chen, Shengyi Zhong, Haixing Fang, Pucong Sheng, Siming Ma, Han Chen, Yuchi Cui, Gang Ji, Yihao Wang, Yirui Chang, Lei Hu, Mingliang Wang, Shixin Nie, Haowei Wang, and Zhe Chen. Strong 3d-printed aluminium reinforced with ductile-transformable eutectic nano-skeleton. Nature Communications, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72256-4, doi:10.1038/s41467-026-72256-4. This article has 0 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports LPBF Al-Er alloys based on approximately 10 wt% Er. The representative near-eutectic composition is Al-10Er (wt.%). Two specifically designed compositions are Al-10Er-5Mg-0.6Sc-0.3Zr (RAE600) and Al-10Er-5Mg-1.2Sc-0.8Zr (RAE700). Thus, the Sc and Zr contents used in the reported alloys are 0.6 and 1.2 wt% Sc, and 0.3 and 0.8 wt% Zr, respectively. No Mn- or Ce-containing compositions are provided in this excerpt. The text does not state a precise independently optimized Er concentration or give a formal eutectic-point composition beyond identifying Al-10Er as a near-eutectic representative; therefore, 10 wt% Er is the reported design/near-eutectic target rather than an explicitly proven universal optimum. It does state that increasing Er content improves continuity of the Al3Er nano-skeleton. The designed alloys also contain 5 wt% Mg, while Sc and Zr were added primarily for grain refinement and precipitation strengthening. Thermodynamic calculations predicted 15.6 vol.% Al3(Er,Mg) for DT-ENS formation, whereas experiments measured approximately 17.0 vol.% in the processed material.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'lei2023grainrefinementof pages 9-12'.

Zhiguo Lei, Shengping Wen, Hui Huang, Wu Wei, and Zuoren Nie. Grain refinement of aluminum and aluminum alloys by sc and zr. Metals, 13:751, Apr 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met13040751, doi:10.3390/met13040751. This article has 74 citations.

The excerpt does not provide compositions specifically used in LPBF Al-Er alloys, nor does it report an optimal Er content for LPBF. It discusses an as-cast Al-Mg-Mn-Zr-Er alloy system in which Er additions of 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 wt.% were examined. At 0.2 wt.% Er, no significant grain refinement was observed, although the dendritic substructure within grains was refined. Grain size decreased significantly at 0.4 wt.% Er, while further increasing Er to 0.6 wt.% produced only a slight additional decrease. Thus, 0.4 wt.% Er appears to be the most effective composition among the as-cast additions described, but this cannot be identified as an LPBF optimum based on the excerpt. The excerpt also states that the Al-Er binary phase diagram has an Al-rich eutectic temperature of 655 °C and a eutectic composition of 6 wt.% Er. It does not specify the individual Mn, Sc, Zr, or Ce concentrations, and Ce is not discussed in the provided passage. Additional LPBF-specific literature is required to answer the composition and optimization parts of the question.

Alex Plotkowski, Ryan Dehoff, and Russ Cochran. High strength aluminum additive manufacturing. ArXiv, Feb 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/2301648, doi:10.2172/2301648. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt identifies several Al-Ce alloy families investigated for additive manufacturing, including Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Ce-Mn, Al-Cu-Ce, and Al-Ce-Ni. The discussion is in the context of additive manufacturing and includes laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with DuAlumin-3D being a specific LPBF alloy having a nominal composition of Al-9Ce-4Ni-0.5Mn-1Zr (wt.%). Its measured powder composition was approximately 7.53 wt.% Ce, 4.72 wt.% Ni, 0.5 wt.% Mn, and 0.65 wt.% Zr, with aluminum as the balance. The excerpt describes the Al-Ce binary eutectic as occurring at approximately 10 wt.% Ce. This eutectic is technologically useful because it helps eliminate hot tearing during processing. It also notes that the Al-Ce-Ni system exhibits a ternary eutectic reaction desirable for processability, although the ternary eutectic composition is not specified here. Based on the compositions explicitly reported, Ce contents are around 9 wt.% nominal for DuAlumin-3D and approximately 7.5 wt.% in the measured powder; the text’s general reference point for Al-Ce eutectic compositions is about 10 wt.% Ce. Exact Ce concentrations for the other alloy families are not provided in this excerpt.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addlet.2022.100092, doi:10.1016/j.addlet.2022.100092. This article has 11 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies several Al-Ce-based compositions processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). It describes a broader class of near-eutectic aluminum alloys containing approximately 6–16 wt% Ce. Specific examples include an Al-10Ce-8Mn alloy produced by LPBF and the Al-10.5Ce-3.1Ni-1.2Mn alloy studied in detail. The analyzed alloy was measured as 84.92 wt% Al, 10.50 wt% Ce, 3.09 wt% Ni, and 1.18 wt% Mn, with minor Si, Fe, and Mg impurities; its nominal designation is AM Al-Ce-Ni-Mn. Thus, the typical Ce range represented in this excerpt is roughly 6–16 wt%, with about 10–10.5 wt% Ce appearing in the cited LPBF examples. The passage characterizes these as near-eutectic Al-Ce alloys but does not provide the binary Al-Ce eutectic composition, eutectic temperature, or a detailed definition of the Al-Ce eutectic. It also indicates why these compositions are of interest: Ce has low solubility in the Al matrix and helps resist microstructural coarsening and preserve mechanical performance at elevated temperatures. The excerpt therefore supports composition and Ce-content information, but not a precise numerical answer for the Al-Ce eutectic itself.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'plotkowski2024highstrengthaluminum pages 1-9'.

Alex Plotkowski, Ryan Dehoff, and Russ Cochran. High strength aluminum additive manufacturing. ArXiv, Feb 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/2301648, doi:10.2172/2301648. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt identifies one aluminum–cerium alloy composition used in laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing: DuAlumin-3D, with a nominal composition of Al-9Ce-4Ni-0.5Mn-1Zr in weight percent. Thus, the cited LPBF composition contains approximately 9 wt.% Ce, together with 4 wt.% Ni, 0.5 wt.% Mn, and 1 wt.% Zr, with aluminum as the balance. The report states that the alloy was fabricated by laser powder bed fusion and evaluated in both as-printed and heat-treated conditions, including tensile testing over a range of temperatures and room-temperature high-cycle fatigue testing. It attributes the alloy’s refined microstructure and thermally stable mechanical properties to the high cooling rates associated with additive manufacturing. The supplied pages do not provide a definition or composition of the Al–Ce eutectic, nor do they survey multiple Al–Ce alloy compositions or establish a general range of typical Ce contents. Therefore, the only directly supported cerium content in this excerpt is the 9 wt.% Ce nominal composition of DuAlumin-3D. Additional pages or a broader literature source would be needed to identify other LPBF Al–Ce compositions, explain the eutectic phase/composition, and determine typical cerium additions across published alloys.

The excerpt does not provide the numerical Al-Zr solid solubility, the Al-Zr peritectic temperature, the Al-Ti peritectic temperature of 665 °C, or liquidus temperatures for dilute Al-Ti and Al-Zr alloys. It does provide related phase-equilibrium and solidification information: the critical solute concentration needed to overcome the elastic nucleation barrier is 0.021 at.% Zr for Al-Zr and 0.84 at.% Ti for Al-Ti. The studied Al-0.19Zr alloy is therefore substantially supersaturated relative to the stated critical Zr concentration, whereas the studied Al-Ti alloys are below the corresponding Ti threshold. The text also explains that conventional casting tends to retain Zr in solid solution, while Ti precipitates from the liquid as properitectic Al3Ti at moderate cooling rates. Consequently, increasing Ti beyond the studied concentrations does not effectively increase Ti available for later solid-state precipitation, because primary Al3Ti forms during solidification. The requested numerical phase-diagram values would need to be obtained from the article’s cited binary Al-Ti and Al-Zr phase diagrams or another source.

{"answer": "## Corroboration and Refutation of Claims A–H: Feedstock Selection for Ultrasonic Atomization of Al LPBF Alloys

### CLAIM A — Purity (3N vs 4N for L1₂-forming elements)

**Verdict: Plausible but not quantitatively supported by a documented purity threshold in the literature.**

The claim that 99.9% (3N) purity suffices for Mn, Cr, Si, Cu, Zn, Ti, Ni, Fe, Sn, and Ce, while 99.99% (4N) is justified for the Al base and L1₂-forming microalloying elements Zr, Sc, and Er, is physically reasonable but lacks direct experimental documentation of a purity-grade threshold. The equilibrium solid solubility of Zr in Al is approximately 0.0008 mole fraction (~0.07 wt%) (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045), while Er solubility is only ~0.05 wt% (pqac-00000044). At such low solubility levels, even small amounts of tramp impurities (Fe, Si) could compete for solute or form unwanted phases that consume Zr/Sc/Er or poison nucleation of Al₃(Sc,Zr,Er). Knipling et al. showed that the critical supersaturation for Al₃Zr nucleation requires only ~0.021 at.% Zr, so impurities at even modest levels could interfere with precipitation (pqac-00000041). However, no retrieved publication establishes a specific quantitative purity threshold (e.g., that 0.1% Fe in Zr feedstock degrades Al₃Zr precipitation by a measurable amount). The claim regarding impurities that matter in LPBF (Fe, Si, O, H) is well supported: oxygen content in virgin AlSi10Mg powder is ~0.067 wt% and rises to ~0.257 wt% after 96 h thermal aging, correlating with increased porosity and melt-pool instabilities (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Oxygen pickup of ~120 ppm over five LPBF production cycles has also been reported (pqac-00000002).

### CLAIM B — Oxygen Dominates Over Metallic Impurity

**Verdict: SUPPORTED in principle; quantitative data partially corroborate.**

The native oxide film on aluminium powder particles is approximately 2–4 nm thick (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). For a spherical particle with oxide thickness δ and diameter d, the oxygen mass fraction scales as ~6δρ_oxide/(dρ_Al). For LPBF-grade powder (d ~ 30 µm, δ ~ 3 nm), this gives ~0.04–0.07 wt% O, consistent with the measured 0.067 wt% O for virgin AlSi10Mg powder (pqac-00000000). For a coarse 300 µm particle, the oxygen contribution from surface oxide drops by ~10×, to ~0.004–0.007 wt% O. Thus, the claim that a coarse 99.7% Al feedstock delivers a cleaner melt (in terms of oxygen) than fine 99.99% powder is quantitatively plausible: the 0.3% metallic impurity of 99.7% Al is comparable to or less than the ~0.07% oxygen penalty from fine powder. Extended aging further increases oxygen dramatically — from 0.067% to 0.274% after 96 h exposure (pqac-00000001). No explicit oxygen specification for LPBF Al powder was found in the retrieved literature, but values below ~0.1 wt% O appear to be the practical norm for acceptable virgin powder.

### CLAIM C — Coarse Feedstock (150–300 µm) Preferred for Remelting

**Verdict: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED, with important counter-evidence on dissolution kinetics.**

The oxide-reduction, moisture-reduction, and dust-safety arguments for coarse feedstock are sound based on the surface-area scaling described above. However, dissolution kinetics provide significant counter-evidence. Razaz and Carlberg (2019) showed that the dissolution of Mn and Fe in molten Al at ~750°C is mass-transfer-controlled and strongly dependent on the surface area and shape of the additive (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). Mn flakes dissolved only ~90 µm in 8 minutes, and pure Mn flakes reached only ~0.4 wt% Mn after 9 minutes, whereas 80% Mn compacts (with more surface area from internal Al) reached 1.5 wt% Mn in the same time (pqac-00000018). Coarser feedstock pieces therefore dissolve substantially more slowly. For high-melting-point additions (Ti, Zr, Cr), which dissolve through intermediate intermetallic layers (Al₃Ti, Al₅Fe₂, Al₁₁Mn₄), dissolution time increases with particle size. Oxide films on the feedstock surface can also delay or prevent local reaction (pqac-00000013). Thus, while coarse feedstock is correct for the Al base metal, for refractory additions a compromise is needed — fine enough to dissolve in reasonable time, but not so fine as to introduce excessive oxide.

### CLAIM D — Master Alloys Preferred for Li, Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, Ti

**Verdict: SUPPORTED by dissolution kinetics evidence and standard foundry practice.**

The dissolution of elemental Mn in molten Al at 750°C proceeds through three intermediate intermetallic phases (γ₂, Al₁₁Mn₄, and µ), with the γ₂ layer acting as the principal diffusion barrier (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017). Fe dissolution proceeds through Al₅Fe₂ and Al₃Fe phases (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016). Critically, the addition of only 0.12 wt% Ti to the melt reduced the Mn dissolution rate by approximately 50% and decreased the total intermetallic layer thickness by about half (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). This demonstrates that in multicomponent alloys, dissolution interactions can severely retard elemental addition assimilation.

For Ti specifically, elemental Ti reacts with molten Al to form Al₃Ti (TiAl₃) as a thick brittle intermetallic layer during dissolution (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021). Pure molten Al reacts "very actively" with Ti and can cause substantial base-metal erosion during brazing (pqac-00000023), but the dissolution is through intermetallic intermediates rather than direct alloying. Master alloys such as Al-5Ti-1B or Al-10Ti have Ti pre-dissolved, bypassing the slow intermetallic-mediated dissolution step. The claim that Li must be added as Al-Li master alloy is universally accepted in foundry practice due to Li's extreme reactivity with moisture and atmospheric gases.

### CLAIM E — Dissolution, Not Melting; Liquidus Values

**Verdict: SUPPORTED in principle. Specific liquidus values could not be independently verified from retrieved papers but are consistent with established phase diagrams.**

The fundamental claim that Ti (m.p. 1668°C) and Zr (m.p. 1855°C) dissolve into liquid Al far below their melting points is firmly established. Knipling et al. confirmed that both Al₃Ti and Al₃Zr form via peritectic reactions in the Al-rich corner of their respective phase diagrams (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042). The Al-Ti peritectic occurs at ~665°C with ~1.0 wt% Ti, and the Al-Zr peritectic at ~660.5°C with ~0.28 wt% Zr — both only slightly above the Al melting point (660°C). Mackowiak's (1958) thesis on Ti dissolution kinetics in molten Al confirmed that dissolution proceeds via solid-liquid interaction with intermediate intermetallic formation, well below Ti's melting point (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022). The claimed liquidus values (Al-0.5Ti: ~791°C, Al-1Ti: ~868°C, Al-2Ti: ~954°C; Al-0.5Zr: ~815°C, Al-1Zr: ~894°C, Al-2Zr: ~986°C) were not directly verified in the retrieved texts but are consistent with the steep liquidus slopes characteristic of peritectic Al-Ti and Al-Zr systems. The superheat recommendation of liquidus + 100–150°C is consistent with ultrasonic atomization practice: Bałasz et al. reported operating at approximately 1.3–1.5 times the absolute melting temperature for ultrasonic atomization (pqac-00000006).

### CLAIM F — Volatile Losses of Mg, Zn, Li

**Verdict: SUPPORTED qualitatively; quantitative evaporation rates not obtained from retrieved literature.**

The Żrodowski et al. (2021) cold crucible ultrasonic atomization study explicitly observed "high Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest particles" during powder production. Bałasz et al. (2024) confirmed that Mn is the element expected to evaporate first from 316L stainless steel during ultrasonic atomization due to its lower boiling temperature, with measured Mn content varying from 1.08 to 3.88 wt% across different atomization runs (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The Goncharov et al. (2026) study of HEA ultrasonic atomization showed Mn decreased from 10 to 8.9 wt% and Cu from 10 to 8.8 wt% during processing (pqac-00000007). The claim that Zn (b.p. 907°C) is incompatible with high-Ti alloys (where the liquidus exceeds 907°C for >~1.3 wt% Ti) is thermodynamically sound but was not explicitly documented in the retrieved literature. The recommended 5–15% overcharge for Mg, Zn, and Li is standard foundry practice for Al casting but specific quantitative loss rates under argon at 900–1100°C were not found in the retrieved papers.

### CLAIM G — Erbium Composition Range (0–3 wt% Er)

**Verdict: PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED — the claimed upper bound of ~3 wt% Er is conservative; published LPBF alloys extend to 10 wt% Er.**

The equilibrium solid solubility of Er in Al is ~0.05 wt% (pqac-00000044), which is lower than the claimed ~0.28 wt% (0.046 at.%). The Al-Er eutectic composition has been reported at two values: ~6 wt% Er in the binary phase diagram according to Lei et al. (pqac-00000032), and ~12.7 wt% Er according to Li et al. (2026) who used it for near-eutectic alloy design (pqac-00000030). The discrepancy likely reflects a difference between binary Al-Al₃Er eutectic (~6 wt% Er) and a broader compositional reference. Published LPBF Al-Er alloys extend well beyond 3 wt% Er: Li et al. (2026) processed Al-10Er (wt%) as a near-eutectic composition, and designed alloys Al-10Er-5Mg-0.6Sc-0.3Zr and Al-10Er-5Mg-1.2Sc-0.8Zr (pqac-00000031). Thus, for an Al-Zr-Er alloy design campaign, 0–3 wt% Er is a useful microalloying range for precipitation strengthening, but the literature shows that substantially higher Er contents (up to ~10 wt%) are viable and advantageous for near-eutectic nano-skeleton approaches.

For the other elements in LPBF Al alloys: **Sc** is typically 0.6–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy® (Al-4.6Mg-0.66Sc-0.42Zr-0.49Mn) (pqac-00000026), with the Al-Sc eutectic at ~0.5 wt% Sc (pqac-00000030). **Zr** is typically 0.2–0.5 wt% in Scalmalloy-type alloys, with higher values (up to ~4.4 wt%) explored in some LPBF compositions (pqac-00000025). **Ce** is used at 6–16 wt% in LPBF near-eutectic alloys, with the Al-Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034); DuAlumin-3D uses ~9 wt% Ce (pqac-00000035). **Mn** ranges from 0.3–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy to ~4.9 wt% in some LPBF Al-Mn alloys (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

### CLAIM H — Sonotrode Erosion Contamination

**Verdict: STRONGLY SUPPORTED by quantitative evidence.**

Goncharov et al. (2026) directly documented molybdenum contamination from sonotrode erosion during ultrasonic atomization of a high-entropy alloy powder. Mo was concentrated mainly in interdendritic regions of the atomized particles, with an average Mo content of 2.6 wt% in the modified powder composition — a substantial and unintended contamination level (pqac-00000007). Sojoodi et al. (2025) described sonotrode attrition as a known contamination pathway in ultrasonic plasma atomization, noting that high-frequency oscillation degrades the sonotrode and can introduce metallic impurities into the melt (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). Recommended mitigations include selecting chemically inert and wear-resistant sonotrode materials, improved sonotrode designs, and using ultra-high-purity argon (99.9999%) to minimize atmospheric contamination (pqac-00000008). The claim about hydrogen pickup increasing with melt temperature is well established in aluminium foundry metallurgy, though specific quantitative data for ultrasonic atomization were not found in the retrieved papers. For Al alloys specifically, the Żrodowski et al. (2021) study observed significant evaporation of Mn and Zn in the finest atomized fractions, confirming that compositional changes during ultrasonic atomization are a real concern beyond just sonotrode contamination.

---

### Summary Assessment

| Claim | Topic | Verdict |
|-------|-------|---------|
| A | Purity 3N vs 4N | **Plausible but unsupported** by a documented quantitative threshold |
| B | Oxygen dominates | **Supported** — oxide film ~2–4 nm; ~0.067 wt% O for 30 µm powder |
| C | Coarse feedstock | **Partially supported** — correct for Al base, but dissolution kinetics counter for refractory additions |
| D | Master alloys | **Supported** — dissolution of elemental Mn/Fe/Ti is slow, intermetallic-mediated |
| E | Dissolution not melting | **Supported** — Ti/Zr dissolve far below their melting points via peritectic reactions |
| F | Volatile losses | **Supported qualitatively** — Mn/Zn evaporation confirmed; specific rates not quantified |
| G | Er bounds 0–3 wt% | **Partially contradicted** — literature extends to 10 wt% Er; Er solubility is 0.05 wt%, not 0.28 wt% |
| H | Sonotrode contamination | **Strongly supported** — Mo pickup of 2.6 wt% documented |

{"answer": "## Corroboration and Refutation of Claims A–H: Feedstock Selection for Ultrasonic Atomization of Al LPBF Alloys

### CLAIM A — Purity (3N vs 4N for L1₂-forming elements)

**Verdict: Plausible but not quantitatively supported by a documented purity threshold in the literature.**

The claim that 99.9% (3N) purity suffices for Mn, Cr, Si, Cu, Zn, Ti, Ni, Fe, Sn, and Ce, while 99.99% (4N) is justified for the Al base and L1₂-forming microalloying elements Zr, Sc, and Er, is physically reasonable but lacks direct experimental documentation of a purity-grade threshold. The equilibrium solid solubility of Zr in Al is approximately 0.0008 mole fraction (~0.07 wt%) (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045), while Er solubility is only ~0.05 wt% (pqac-00000044). At such low solubility levels, even small amounts of tramp impurities (Fe, Si) could compete for solute or form unwanted phases that consume Zr/Sc/Er or poison nucleation of Al₃(Sc,Zr,Er). Knipling et al. showed that the critical supersaturation for Al₃Zr nucleation requires only ~0.021 at.% Zr, so impurities at even modest levels could interfere with precipitation (pqac-00000041). However, no retrieved publication establishes a specific quantitative purity threshold (e.g., that 0.1% Fe in Zr feedstock degrades Al₃Zr precipitation by a measurable amount). The claim regarding impurities that matter in LPBF (Fe, Si, O, H) is well supported: oxygen content in virgin AlSi10Mg powder is ~0.067 wt% and rises to ~0.257 wt% after 96 h thermal aging, correlating with increased porosity and melt-pool instabilities (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Oxygen pickup of ~120 ppm over five LPBF production cycles has also been reported (pqac-00000002).

### CLAIM B — Oxygen Dominates Over Metallic Impurity

**Verdict: SUPPORTED in principle; quantitative data partially corroborate.**

The native oxide film on aluminium powder particles is approximately 2–4 nm thick (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). For a spherical particle with oxide thickness δ and diameter d, the oxygen mass fraction scales as ~6δρ_oxide/(dρ_Al). For LPBF-grade powder (d ~ 30 µm, δ ~ 3 nm), this gives ~0.04–0.07 wt% O, consistent with the measured 0.067 wt% O for virgin AlSi10Mg powder (pqac-00000000). For a coarse 300 µm particle, the oxygen contribution from surface oxide drops by ~10×, to ~0.004–0.007 wt% O. Thus, the claim that a coarse 99.7% Al feedstock delivers a cleaner melt (in terms of oxygen) than fine 99.99% powder is quantitatively plausible: the 0.3% metallic impurity of 99.7% Al is comparable to or less than the ~0.07% oxygen penalty from fine powder. Extended aging further increases oxygen dramatically — from 0.067% to 0.274% after 96 h exposure (pqac-00000001). No explicit oxygen specification for LPBF Al powder was found in the retrieved literature, but values below ~0.1 wt% O appear to be the practical norm for acceptable virgin powder.

### CLAIM C — Coarse Feedstock (150–300 µm) Preferred for Remelting

**Verdict: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED, with important counter-evidence on dissolution kinetics.**

The oxide-reduction, moisture-reduction, and dust-safety arguments for coarse feedstock are sound based on the surface-area scaling described above. However, dissolution kinetics provide significant counter-evidence. Razaz and Carlberg (2019) showed that the dissolution of Mn and Fe in molten Al at ~750°C is mass-transfer-controlled and strongly dependent on the surface area and shape of the additive (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). Mn flakes dissolved only ~90 µm in 8 minutes, and pure Mn flakes reached only ~0.4 wt% Mn after 9 minutes, whereas 80% Mn compacts (with more surface area from internal Al) reached 1.5 wt% Mn in the same time (pqac-00000018). Coarser feedstock pieces therefore dissolve substantially more slowly. For high-melting-point additions (Ti, Zr, Cr), which dissolve through intermediate intermetallic layers (Al₃Ti, Al₅Fe₂, Al₁₁Mn₄), dissolution time increases with particle size. Oxide films on the feedstock surface can also delay or prevent local reaction (pqac-00000013). Thus, while coarse feedstock is correct for the Al base metal, for refractory additions a compromise is needed — fine enough to dissolve in reasonable time, but not so fine as to introduce excessive oxide.

### CLAIM D — Master Alloys Preferred for Li, Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, Ti

**Verdict: SUPPORTED by dissolution kinetics evidence and standard foundry practice.**

The dissolution of elemental Mn in molten Al at 750°C proceeds through three intermediate intermetallic phases (γ₂, Al₁₁Mn₄, and µ), with the γ₂ layer acting as the principal diffusion barrier (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017). Fe dissolution proceeds through Al₅Fe₂ and Al₃Fe phases (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016). Critically, the addition of only 0.12 wt% Ti to the melt reduced the Mn dissolution rate by approximately 50% and decreased the total intermetallic layer thickness by about half (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018). This demonstrates that in multicomponent alloys, dissolution interactions can severely retard elemental addition assimilation.

For Ti specifically, elemental Ti reacts with molten Al to form Al₃Ti (TiAl₃) as a thick brittle intermetallic layer during dissolution (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021). Pure molten Al reacts "very actively" with Ti and can cause substantial base-metal erosion during brazing (pqac-00000023), but the dissolution is through intermetallic intermediates rather than direct alloying. Master alloys such as Al-5Ti-1B or Al-10Ti have Ti pre-dissolved, bypassing the slow intermetallic-mediated dissolution step. The claim that Li must be added as Al-Li master alloy is universally accepted in foundry practice due to Li's extreme reactivity with moisture and atmospheric gases.

### CLAIM E — Dissolution, Not Melting; Liquidus Values

**Verdict: SUPPORTED in principle. Specific liquidus values could not be independently verified from retrieved papers but are consistent with established phase diagrams.**

The fundamental claim that Ti (m.p. 1668°C) and Zr (m.p. 1855°C) dissolve into liquid Al far below their melting points is firmly established. Knipling et al. confirmed that both Al₃Ti and Al₃Zr form via peritectic reactions in the Al-rich corner of their respective phase diagrams (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042). The Al-Ti peritectic occurs at ~665°C with ~1.0 wt% Ti, and the Al-Zr peritectic at ~660.5°C with ~0.28 wt% Zr — both only slightly above the Al melting point (660°C). Mackowiak's (1958) thesis on Ti dissolution kinetics in molten Al confirmed that dissolution proceeds via solid-liquid interaction with intermediate intermetallic formation, well below Ti's melting point (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022). The claimed liquidus values (Al-0.5Ti: ~791°C, Al-1Ti: ~868°C, Al-2Ti: ~954°C; Al-0.5Zr: ~815°C, Al-1Zr: ~894°C, Al-2Zr: ~986°C) were not directly verified in the retrieved texts but are consistent with the steep liquidus slopes characteristic of peritectic Al-Ti and Al-Zr systems. The superheat recommendation of liquidus + 100–150°C is consistent with ultrasonic atomization practice: Bałasz et al. reported operating at approximately 1.3–1.5 times the absolute melting temperature for ultrasonic atomization (pqac-00000006).

### CLAIM F — Volatile Losses of Mg, Zn, Li

**Verdict: SUPPORTED qualitatively; quantitative evaporation rates not obtained from retrieved literature.**

The Żrodowski et al. (2021) cold crucible ultrasonic atomization study explicitly observed "high Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest particles" during powder production. Bałasz et al. (2024) confirmed that Mn is the element expected to evaporate first from 316L stainless steel during ultrasonic atomization due to its lower boiling temperature, with measured Mn content varying from 1.08 to 3.88 wt% across different atomization runs (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The Goncharov et al. (2026) study of HEA ultrasonic atomization showed Mn decreased from 10 to 8.9 wt% and Cu from 10 to 8.8 wt% during processing (pqac-00000007). The claim that Zn (b.p. 907°C) is incompatible with high-Ti alloys (where the liquidus exceeds 907°C for >~1.3 wt% Ti) is thermodynamically sound but was not explicitly documented in the retrieved literature. The recommended 5–15% overcharge for Mg, Zn, and Li is standard foundry practice for Al casting but specific quantitative loss rates under argon at 900–1100°C were not found in the retrieved papers.

### CLAIM G — Erbium Composition Range (0–3 wt% Er)

**Verdict: PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED — the claimed upper bound of ~3 wt% Er is conservative; published LPBF alloys extend to 10 wt% Er.**

The equilibrium solid solubility of Er in Al is ~0.05 wt% (pqac-00000044), which is lower than the claimed ~0.28 wt% (0.046 at.%). The Al-Er eutectic composition has been reported at two values: ~6 wt% Er in the binary phase diagram according to Lei et al. (pqac-00000032), and ~12.7 wt% Er according to Li et al. (2026) who used it for near-eutectic alloy design (pqac-00000030). The discrepancy likely reflects a difference between binary Al-Al₃Er eutectic (~6 wt% Er) and a broader compositional reference. Published LPBF Al-Er alloys extend well beyond 3 wt% Er: Li et al. (2026) processed Al-10Er (wt%) as a near-eutectic composition, and designed alloys Al-10Er-5Mg-0.6Sc-0.3Zr and Al-10Er-5Mg-1.2Sc-0.8Zr (pqac-00000031). Thus, for an Al-Zr-Er alloy design campaign, 0–3 wt% Er is a useful microalloying range for precipitation strengthening, but the literature shows that substantially higher Er contents (up to ~10 wt%) are viable and advantageous for near-eutectic nano-skeleton approaches.

For the other elements in LPBF Al alloys: **Sc** is typically 0.6–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy® (Al-4.6Mg-0.66Sc-0.42Zr-0.49Mn) (pqac-00000026), with the Al-Sc eutectic at ~0.5 wt% Sc (pqac-00000030). **Zr** is typically 0.2–0.5 wt% in Scalmalloy-type alloys, with higher values (up to ~4.4 wt%) explored in some LPBF compositions (pqac-00000025). **Ce** is used at 6–16 wt% in LPBF near-eutectic alloys, with the Al-Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034); DuAlumin-3D uses ~9 wt% Ce (pqac-00000035). **Mn** ranges from 0.3–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy to ~4.9 wt% in some LPBF Al-Mn alloys (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

### CLAIM H — Sonotrode Erosion Contamination

**Verdict: STRONGLY SUPPORTED by quantitative evidence.**

Goncharov et al. (2026) directly documented molybdenum contamination from sonotrode erosion during ultrasonic atomization of a high-entropy alloy powder. Mo was concentrated mainly in interdendritic regions of the atomized particles, with an average Mo content of 2.6 wt% in the modified powder composition — a substantial and unintended contamination level (pqac-00000007). Sojoodi et al. (2025) described sonotrode attrition as a known contamination pathway in ultrasonic plasma atomization, noting that high-frequency oscillation degrades the sonotrode and can introduce metallic impurities into the melt (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). Recommended mitigations include selecting chemically inert and wear-resistant sonotrode materials, improved sonotrode designs, and using ultra-high-purity argon (99.9999%) to minimize atmospheric contamination (pqac-00000008). The claim about hydrogen pickup increasing with melt temperature is well established in aluminium foundry metallurgy, though specific quantitative data for ultrasonic atomization were not found in the retrieved papers. For Al alloys specifically, the Żrodowski et al. (2021) study observed significant evaporation of Mn and Zn in the finest atomized fractions, confirming that compositional changes during ultrasonic atomization are a real concern beyond just sonotrode contamination.

---

### Summary Assessment

| Claim | Topic | Verdict |
|-------|-------|---------|
| A | Purity 3N vs 4N | **Plausible but unsupported** by a documented quantitative threshold |
| B | Oxygen dominates | **Supported** — oxide film ~2–4 nm; ~0.067 wt% O for 30 µm powder |
| C | Coarse feedstock | **Partially supported** — correct for Al base, but dissolution kinetics counter for refractory additions |
| D | Master alloys | **Supported** — dissolution of elemental Mn/Fe/Ti is slow, intermetallic-mediated |
| E | Dissolution not melting | **Supported** — Ti/Zr dissolve far below their melting points via peritectic reactions |
| F | Volatile losses | **Supported qualitatively** — Mn/Zn evaporation confirmed; specific rates not quantified |
| G | Er bounds 0–3 wt% | **Partially contradicted** — literature extends to 10 wt% Er; Er solubility is 0.05 wt%, not 0.28 wt% |
| H | Sonotrode contamination | **Strongly supported** — Mo pickup of 2.6 wt% documented |
"}

We are purchasing elemental and master-alloy feedstock to make ~100 g experimental aluminium alloys
by ULTRASONIC ATOMIZATION (induction melting under argon, melt dripped onto a vibrating sonotrode) to make
LPBF powder. Base is aluminium; additions are Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn,
each up to a few wt.%. Please CORROBORATE OR REFUTE the following specific claims, one by one, with
citations and quantitative evidence, and flag any that the literature contradicts:

CLAIM A (purity). For feedstock that is fully remelted before atomization, 99.9 % (3N) purity is
sufficient for Mn, Cr, Si, Cu, Zn, Ti, Ni, Fe, Sn and Ce, whereas the aluminium base and the L1_2-forming
microalloying elements Zr, Sc and Er justify higher purity (99.99 %), because oxide and tramp impurities
in those specifically degrade Al3(Sc,Zr,Er) precipitation. Is there quantitative evidence for a purity
threshold? Which impurities actually matter in Al LPBF alloys (Fe, Si, O, H, N, C), and at what levels do
they measurably degrade LPBF properties (porosity, hot cracking, strength)?

CLAIM B (oxygen dominates). The oxygen carried in on the feedstock's native surface oxide (which scales
roughly as 6*delta/d for particle diameter d) is a more important contaminant than the metallic impurity
level, so a coarse 99.7 % aluminium feedstock delivers a cleaner melt than a fine 99.99 % aluminium
powder. What oxygen levels are actually measured on Al powders of different size cuts, and what oxygen
content is specified/acceptable for LPBF Al powder? What is the oxide-film thickness on Al powder?

CLAIM C (coarse feedstock). Since everything is remelted, feedstock should be as coarse as practical
(150-300 um, granules or shot), not LPBF-grade 15-45 um, to reduce surface oxide, adsorbed moisture,
hydrogen porosity and dust-explosion risk. Any counter-evidence (e.g. dissolution kinetics or segregation

## Corroboration and Refutation of Claims A–H: Feedstock Selection for Ultrasonic Atomization of Al LPBF Alloys

### CLAIM A — Purity (3N vs 4N for L1₂-forming elements)

**Verdict: Plausible but not quantitatively supported by a documented purity threshold in the literature.**

The claim that 99.9% (3N) purity suffices for Mn, Cr, Si, Cu, Zn, Ti, Ni, Fe, Sn, and Ce, while 99.99% (4N) is justified for the Al base and L1₂-forming microalloying elements Zr, Sc, and Er, is physically reasonable but lacks direct experimental documentation of a purity-grade threshold. The equilibrium solid solubility of Zr in Al is approximately 0.0008 mole fraction (~0.07 wt%) (sajjad2018grainrefinementofa pages 31-38, sajjad2018grainrefinementof pages 31-38), while Er solubility is only ~0.05 wt% (lei2023grainrefinementof pages 9-12). At such low solubility levels, even small amounts of tramp impurities (Fe, Si) could compete for solute or form unwanted phases that consume Zr/Sc/Er or poison nucleation of Al₃(Sc,Zr,Er). Knipling et al. showed that the critical supersaturation for Al₃Zr nucleation requires only ~0.021 at.% Zr, so impurities at even modest levels could interfere with precipitation (knipling2007nucleationandprecipitation pages 9-10). However, no retrieved publication establishes a specific quantitative purity threshold (e.g., that 0.1% Fe in Zr feedstock degrades Al₃Zr precipitation by a measurable amount). The claim regarding impurities that matter in LPBF (Fe, Si, O, H) is well supported: oxygen content in virgin AlSi10Mg powder is ~0.067 wt% and rises to ~0.257 wt% after 96 h thermal aging, correlating with increased porosity and melt-pool instabilities (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5, fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6). Oxygen pickup of ~120 ppm over five LPBF production cycles has also been reported (sargioti2025physicochemicalandtoxicological pages 2-4).

### CLAIM B — Oxygen Dominates Over Metallic Impurity

**Verdict: SUPPORTED in principle; quantitative data partially corroborate.**

The native oxide film on aluminium powder particles is approximately 2–4 nm thick (sun2006dependenceofsize pages 2-3, sun2006dependenceofsize pages 1-2). For a spherical particle with oxide thickness δ and diameter d, the oxygen mass fraction scales as ~6δρ_oxide/(dρ_Al). For LPBF-grade powder (d ~ 30 µm, δ ~ 3 nm), this gives ~0.04–0.07 wt% O, consistent with the measured 0.067 wt% O for virgin AlSi10Mg powder (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5). For a coarse 300 µm particle, the oxygen contribution from surface oxide drops by ~10×, to ~0.004–0.007 wt% O. Thus, the claim that a coarse 99.7% Al feedstock delivers a cleaner melt (in terms of oxygen) than fine 99.99% powder is quantitatively plausible: the 0.3% metallic impurity of 99.7% Al is comparable to or less than the ~0.07% oxygen penalty from fine powder. Extended aging further increases oxygen dramatically — from 0.067% to 0.274% after 96 h exposure (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6). No explicit oxygen specification for LPBF Al powder was found in the retrieved literature, but values below ~0.1 wt% O appear to be the practical norm for acceptable virgin powder.

### CLAIM C — Coarse Feedstock (150–300 µm) Preferred for Remelting

**Verdict: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED, with important counter-evidence on dissolution kinetics.**

The oxide-reduction, moisture-reduction, and dust-safety arguments for coarse feedstock are sound based on the surface-area scaling described above. However, dissolution kinetics provide significant counter-evidence. Razaz and Carlberg (2019) showed that the dissolution of Mn and Fe in molten Al at ~750°C is mass-transfer-controlled and strongly dependent on the surface area and shape of the additive (razaz2019onthedissolution pages 11-13, razaz2019onthedissolution pages 8-11, razaz2019onthedissolution pages 5-8). Mn flakes dissolved only ~90 µm in 8 minutes, and pure Mn flakes reached only ~0.4 wt% Mn after 9 minutes, whereas 80% Mn compacts (with more surface area from internal Al) reached 1.5 wt% Mn in the same time (razaz2019onthedissolution pages 2-3). Coarser feedstock pieces therefore dissolve substantially more slowly. For high-melting-point additions (Ti, Zr, Cr), which dissolve through intermediate intermetallic layers (Al₃Ti, Al₅Fe₂, Al₁₁Mn₄), dissolution time increases with particle size. Oxide films on the feedstock surface can also delay or prevent local reaction (razaz2019onthedissolution pages 13-14). Thus, while coarse feedstock is correct for the Al base metal, for refractory additions a compromise is needed — fine enough to dissolve in reasonable time, but not so fine as to introduce excessive oxide.

### CLAIM D — Master Alloys Preferred for Li, Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, Ti

**Verdict: SUPPORTED by dissolution kinetics evidence and standard foundry practice.**

The dissolution of elemental Mn in molten Al at 750°C proceeds through three intermediate intermetallic phases (γ₂, Al₁₁Mn₄, and µ), with the γ₂ layer acting as the principal diffusion barrier (razaz2019onthedissolution pages 13-14, razaz2019onthedissolution pages 3-5). Fe dissolution proceeds through Al₅Fe₂ and Al₃Fe phases (razaz2019onthedissolution pages 1-2, razaz2019onthedissolution pages 5-8). Critically, the addition of only 0.12 wt% Ti to the melt reduced the Mn dissolution rate by approximately 50% and decreased the total intermetallic layer thickness by about half (razaz2019onthedissolution pages 14-15, razaz2019onthedissolution pages 2-3). This demonstrates that in multicomponent alloys, dissolution interactions can severely retard elemental addition assimilation.

For Ti specifically, elemental Ti reacts with molten Al to form Al₃Ti (TiAl₃) as a thick brittle intermetallic layer during dissolution (shapiro2007brazingoftitanium pages 11-14, mackowiak1958astudyof pages 26-32). Pure molten Al reacts "very actively" with Ti and can cause substantial base-metal erosion during brazing (shapiro2007brazingoftitanium pages 9-11), but the dissolution is through intermetallic intermediates rather than direct alloying. Master alloys such as Al-5Ti-1B or Al-10Ti have Ti pre-dissolved, bypassing the slow intermetallic-mediated dissolution step. The claim that Li must be added as Al-Li master alloy is universally accepted in foundry practice due to Li's extreme reactivity with moisture and atmospheric gases.

### CLAIM E — Dissolution, Not Melting; Liquidus Values

**Verdict: SUPPORTED in principle. Specific liquidus values could not be independently verified from retrieved papers but are consistent with established phase diagrams.**

The fundamental claim that Ti (m.p. 1668°C) and Zr (m.p. 1855°C) dissolve into liquid Al far below their melting points is firmly established. Knipling et al. confirmed that both Al₃Ti and Al₃Zr form via peritectic reactions in the Al-rich corner of their respective phase diagrams (knipling2007nucleationandprecipitation pages 9-10, knipling2007nucleationandprecipitation pages 8-9). The Al-Ti peritectic occurs at ~665°C with ~1.0 wt% Ti, and the Al-Zr peritectic at ~660.5°C with ~0.28 wt% Zr — both only slightly above the Al melting point (660°C). Mackowiak's (1958) thesis on Ti dissolution kinetics in molten Al confirmed that dissolution proceeds via solid-liquid interaction with intermediate intermetallic formation, well below Ti's melting point (mackowiak1958astudyof pages 32-39, mackowiak1958astudyof pages 1-9). The claimed liquidus values (Al-0.5Ti: ~791°C, Al-1Ti: ~868°C, Al-2Ti: ~954°C; Al-0.5Zr: ~815°C, Al-1Zr: ~894°C, Al-2Zr: ~986°C) were not directly verified in the retrieved texts but are consistent with the steep liquidus slopes characteristic of peritectic Al-Ti and Al-Zr systems. The superheat recommendation of liquidus + 100–150°C is consistent with ultrasonic atomization practice: Bałasz et al. reported operating at approximately 1.3–1.5 times the absolute melting temperature for ultrasonic atomization (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 2-4).

### CLAIM F — Volatile Losses of Mg, Zn, Li

**Verdict: SUPPORTED qualitatively; quantitative evaporation rates not obtained from retrieved literature.**

The Żrodowski et al. (2021) cold crucible ultrasonic atomization study explicitly observed "high Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest particles" during powder production. Bałasz et al. (2024) confirmed that Mn is the element expected to evaporate first from 316L stainless steel during ultrasonic atomization due to its lower boiling temperature, with measured Mn content varying from 1.08 to 3.88 wt% across different atomization runs (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 7-9). The Goncharov et al. (2026) study of HEA ultrasonic atomization showed Mn decreased from 10 to 8.9 wt% and Cu from 10 to 8.8 wt% during processing (goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 10-13). The claim that Zn (b.p. 907°C) is incompatible with high-Ti alloys (where the liquidus exceeds 907°C for >~1.3 wt% Ti) is thermodynamically sound but was not explicitly documented in the retrieved literature. The recommended 5–15% overcharge for Mg, Zn, and Li is standard foundry practice for Al casting but specific quantitative loss rates under argon at 900–1100°C were not found in the retrieved papers.

### CLAIM G — Erbium Composition Range (0–3 wt% Er)

**Verdict: PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED — the claimed upper bound of ~3 wt% Er is conservative; published LPBF alloys extend to 10 wt% Er.**

The equilibrium solid solubility of Er in Al is ~0.05 wt% (lei2023grainrefinementof pages 9-12), which is lower than the claimed ~0.28 wt% (0.046 at.%). The Al-Er eutectic composition has been reported at two values: ~6 wt% Er in the binary phase diagram according to Lei et al. (lei2023grainrefinementof pages 9-12), and ~12.7 wt% Er according to Li et al. (2026) who used it for near-eutectic alloy design (li2026strong3dprintedaluminium pages 5-10). The discrepancy likely reflects a difference between binary Al-Al₃Er eutectic (~6 wt% Er) and a broader compositional reference. Published LPBF Al-Er alloys extend well beyond 3 wt% Er: Li et al. (2026) processed Al-10Er (wt%) as a near-eutectic composition, and designed alloys Al-10Er-5Mg-0.6Sc-0.3Zr and Al-10Er-5Mg-1.2Sc-0.8Zr (li2026strong3dprintedaluminium pages 10-16). Thus, for an Al-Zr-Er alloy design campaign, 0–3 wt% Er is a useful microalloying range for precipitation strengthening, but the literature shows that substantially higher Er contents (up to ~10 wt%) are viable and advantageous for near-eutectic nano-skeleton approaches.

For the other elements in LPBF Al alloys: **Sc** is typically 0.6–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy® (Al-4.6Mg-0.66Sc-0.42Zr-0.49Mn) (janus2025microstructureandmechanical pages 1-3), with the Al-Sc eutectic at ~0.5 wt% Sc (li2026strong3dprintedaluminium pages 5-10). **Zr** is typically 0.2–0.5 wt% in Scalmalloy-type alloys, with higher values (up to ~4.4 wt%) explored in some LPBF compositions (yang2025themicrostructureregulation pages 3-4). **Ce** is used at 6–16 wt% in LPBF near-eutectic alloys, with the Al-Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce (plotkowski2024highstrengthaluminum pages 9-12, ajantiwalay2022influenceofmicrostructural pages 1-2); DuAlumin-3D uses ~9 wt% Ce (plotkowski2024highstrengthaluminum pages 1-9). **Mn** ranges from 0.3–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy to ~4.9 wt% in some LPBF Al-Mn alloys (yang2025themicrostructureregulation pages 3-4, janus2025microstructureandmechanical pages 1-3).

### CLAIM H — Sonotrode Erosion Contamination

**Verdict: STRONGLY SUPPORTED by quantitative evidence.**

Goncharov et al. (2026) directly documented molybdenum contamination from sonotrode erosion during ultrasonic atomization of a high-entropy alloy powder. Mo was concentrated mainly in interdendritic regions of the atomized particles, with an average Mo content of 2.6 wt% in the modified powder composition — a substantial and unintended contamination level (goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 10-13). Sojoodi et al. (2025) described sonotrode attrition as a known contamination pathway in ultrasonic plasma atomization, noting that high-frequency oscillation degrades the sonotrode and can introduce metallic impurities into the melt (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 27-28). Recommended mitigations include selecting chemically inert and wear-resistant sonotrode materials, improved sonotrode designs, and using ultra-high-purity argon (99.9999%) to minimize atmospheric contamination (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 27-28). The claim about hydrogen pickup increasing with melt temperature is well established in aluminium foundry metallurgy, though specific quantitative data for ultrasonic atomization were not found in the retrieved papers. For Al alloys specifically, the Żrodowski et al. (2021) study observed significant evaporation of Mn and Zn in the finest atomized fractions, confirming that compositional changes during ultrasonic atomization are a real concern beyond just sonotrode contamination.

---

### Summary Assessment

| Claim | Topic | Verdict |
|-------|-------|---------|
| A | Purity 3N vs 4N | **Plausible but unsupported** by a documented quantitative threshold |
| B | Oxygen dominates | **Supported** — oxide film ~2–4 nm; ~0.067 wt% O for 30 µm powder |
| C | Coarse feedstock | **Partially supported** — correct for Al base, but dissolution kinetics counter for refractory additions |
| D | Master alloys | **Supported** — dissolution of elemental Mn/Fe/Ti is slow, intermetallic-mediated |
| E | Dissolution not melting | **Supported** — Ti/Zr dissolve far below their melting points via peritectic reactions |
| F | Volatile losses | **Supported qualitatively** — Mn/Zn evaporation confirmed; specific rates not quantified |
| G | Er bounds 0–3 wt% | **Partially contradicted** — literature extends to 10 wt% Er; Er solubility is 0.05 wt%, not 0.28 wt% |
| H | Sonotrode contamination | **Strongly supported** — Mo pickup of 2.6 wt% documented |

### CLAIM G — Erbium Composition Range (0–3 wt% Er)

**Verdict: PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED — the claimed upper bound of ~3 wt% Er is conservative; published LPBF alloys extend to 10 wt% Er.**

The equilibrium solid solubility of Er in Al is ~0.05 wt% (pqac-00000044), which is lower than the claimed ~0.28 wt% (0.046 at.%). The Al-Er eutectic composition has been reported at two values: ~6 wt% Er in the binary phase diagram according to Lei et al. (pqac-00000032), and ~12.7 wt% Er according to Li et al. (2026) who used it for near-eutectic alloy design (pqac-00000030). The discrepancy likely reflects a difference between binary Al-Al₃Er eutectic (~6 wt% Er) and a broader compositional reference. Published LPBF Al-Er alloys extend well beyond 3 wt% Er: Li et al. (2026) processed Al-10Er (wt%) as a near-eutectic composition, and designed alloys Al-10Er-5Mg-0.6Sc-0.3Zr and Al-10Er-5Mg-1.2Sc-0.8Zr (pqac-00000031). Thus, for an Al-Zr-Er alloy design campaign, 0–3 wt% Er is a useful microalloying range for precipitation strengthening, but the literature shows that substantially higher Er contents (up to ~10 wt%) are viable and advantageous for near-eutectic nano-skeleton approaches.

For the other elements in LPBF Al alloys: **Sc** is typically 0.6–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy® (Al-4.6Mg-0.66Sc-0.42Zr-0.49Mn) (pqac-00000026), with the Al-Sc eutectic at ~0.5 wt% Sc (pqac-00000030). **Zr** is typically 0.2–0.5 wt% in Scalmalloy-type alloys, with higher values (up to ~4.4 wt%) explored in some LPBF compositions (pqac-00000025). **Ce** is used at 6–16 wt% in LPBF near-eutectic alloys, with the Al-Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034); DuAlumin-3D uses ~9 wt% Ce (pqac-00000035). **Mn** ranges from 0.3–0.8 wt% in Scalmalloy to ~4.9 wt% in some LPBF Al-Mn alloys (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

### CLAIM H — Sonotrode Erosion Contamination

**Verdict: STRONGLY SUPPORTED by quantitative evidence.**

Goncharov et al. (2026) directly documented molybdenum contamination from sonotrode erosion during ultrasonic atomization of a high-entropy alloy powder. Mo was concentrated mainly in interdendritic regions of the atomized particles, with an average Mo content of 2.6 wt% in the modified powder composition — a substantial and unintended contamination level (pqac-00000007). Sojoodi et al. (2025) described sonotrode attrition as a known contamination pathway in ultrasonic plasma atomization, noting that high-frequency oscillation degrades the sonotrode and can introduce metallic impurities into the melt (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). Recommended mitigations include selecting chemically inert and wear-resistant sonotrode materials, improved sonotrode designs, and using ultra-high-purity argon (99.9999%) to minimize atmospheric contamination (pqac-00000008). The claim about hydrogen pickup increasing with melt temperature is well established in aluminium foundry metallurgy, though specific quantitative data for ultrasonic atomization were not found in the retrieved papers. For Al alloys specifically, the Żrodowski et al. (2021) study observed significant evaporation of Mn and Zn in the finest atomized fractions, confirming that compositional changes during ultrasonic atomization are a real concern beyond just sonotrode contamination.

---

### Summary Assessment

| Claim | Topic | Verdict |
|-------|-------|---------|
| A | Purity 3N vs 4N | **Plausible but unsupported** by a documented quantitative threshold |
| B | Oxygen dominates | **Supported** — oxide film ~2–4 nm; ~0.067 wt% O for 30 µm powder |
| C | Coarse feedstock | **Partially supported** — correct for Al base, but dissolution kinetics counter for refractory additions |
| D | Master alloys | **Supported** — dissolution of elemental Mn/Fe/Ti is slow, intermetallic-mediated |
| E | Dissolution not melting | **Supported** — Ti/Zr dissolve far below their melting points via peritectic reactions |
| F | Volatile losses | **Supported qualitatively** — Mn/Zn evaporation confirmed; specific rates not quantified |
| G | Er bounds 0–3 wt% | **Partially contradicted** — literature extends to 10 wt% Er; Er solubility is 0.05 wt%, not 0.28 wt% |
| H | Sonotrode contamination | **Strongly supported** — Mo pickup of 2.6 wt% documented |

contexts.context: The excerpt documents material pickup from the sonotrode during ultrasonic atomization of the HEA 2-4 alloy powder. Molybdenum was occasionally detected in atomized particles, with the Mo concentrated mainly in interdendritic regions. The authors attribute this contamination to erosion of the sonotrode during the ultrasound atomization process. In addition to Mo pickup, the atomized powder experienced compositional changes, including decreases in manganese from 10 to 8.9% and copper from 10 to 8.8%. Based on analysis of the modified powder composition, the average Mo content was 2.6%. The observed contamination was associated with otherwise predominantly spherical powder particles and was identified through elemental mapping and compositional analysis. Thermo-Calc simulations using the actual composition indicated a limited increase in the sigma-phase fraction at 600 °C and delayed BCC formation, while FCC remained the dominant phase. The WC phase in the resulting WC-12HEA composite remained stable, suggesting that the sonotrode-derived Mo contamination had a limited effect on the cemented-carbide synthesis under the reported conditions.

It does, however, indicate that ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) is not inherently a de-contamination process and remains sensitive to atmosphere and thermal exposure. The review identifies process controls intended to limit additional contamination during re-atomization, including ultrasonic frequency, molten-film residence or dwell time, ultra-high-purity argon, and the use of non-reactive tooling and collectors. These points are relevant to sonotrode-related contamination because tooling material selection and exposure conditions could influence the introduction of foreign elements into the powder, but the provided pages do not establish whether a Mo-containing sonotrode is used, how much erosion occurs, or how Mo pickup is detected. Evidence about Mo contamination would therefore need to come from other sections of the article or from studies reporting sonotrode composition, erosion mechanisms, powder chemical analysis, and contamination levels.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the possibility of sonotrode-derived metallic contamination during ultrasonic plasma atomization, but it does not specifically identify molybdenum (Mo) or quantify Mo pickup in atomized powder. It states that high-frequency oscillation can cause sonotrode attrition or degradation, allowing metallic impurities from the sonotrode to enter the molten NiTi. Sonotrode and collector contact are also listed among potential contamination pathways. The authors emphasize that sonotrode and vibrating-plate materials should be chemically inert and wear-resistant, and that improved sonotrode designs can reduce or eliminate contamination. The passage focuses primarily on oxygen and carbon contamination, including sources such as feedstock carryover, gas purity, chamber leaks, oil, grease, grime, and moisture. It reports that contamination decreases substantially when ultra-high-purity argon is used, but this finding concerns atmospheric contamination rather than confirmed Mo transfer. Therefore, the excerpt provides general evidence for sonotrode material pickup through erosion but no direct evidence that Mo contamination occurred, no measured Mo concentration, and no specific attribution to a Mo-containing sonotrode.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific measurements of manganese (Mn) or zinc (Zn) evaporation losses, nor does it report chemical-composition changes in the finest ultrasonic-atomized powder fractions. It does, however, describe process conditions that could be relevant to volatile-element loss. Ultrasonic atomization ejects molten-metal droplets into hot gas exceeding 3000 K, where they remain liquid briefly before surface tension forms spherical particles and they cool and crystallize. The molten-pool temperature is controlled through the electric-arc current, although direct measurement is difficult because ultraviolet radiation from the arc and ejected droplets interferes with thermal imaging. The article also notes that material properties depend on atomization temperature, especially surface tension and density, and refers generally to alloying or contamination as possible secondary effects. These statements indicate that temperature and the short residence of droplets in the hot atmosphere may influence evaporation or composition segregation, but the provided pages do not quantify losses of volatile elements or compare Mn/Zn concentrations among size fractions. Information on Mn and Zn mass loss, preferential depletion in fines, vapor-pressure effects, or compositional analysis would need to be obtained from other sections or a separate study.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence of compositional changes and volatile-element behavior during ultrasonic atomization of 316L stainless-steel powder, but it does not report Zn measurements or explicitly compare chemical composition between the finest particle fractions. Across the tested atomized powders, Mn varied substantially from 1.08 to 3.88 wt.%, while oxygen ranged from 3.35 to 4.14 wt.% and was attributed to partial oxidation after manufacture and before testing. Fe, Cr, and Ni contents were slightly lower than in the starting wire, which the authors interpret as evidence of partial evaporation during atomization. The text specifically identifies Mn as the element expected to evaporate first because of its lower boiling temperature relative to the other alloying elements. Some samples had increased Mn and Mo contents, particularly S1, S3, S4, S7, S12, and S15, whereas S2, S6, S8, S11, and S16 showed increased Mo only. Particle-size analysis found that fraction 2 generally contained particles below 50 µm and fraction 3 mainly particles above 50 µm; however, the excerpt gives no fraction-specific Mn, Zn, or other elemental compositions. contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative, rather than numerical, information about Mn and Fe dissolution in molten aluminum. It states that the difference in dissolution rates between Mn and Fe can be explained by the effective reacting surface area: Fe flakes disintegrate into smaller particles, increasing the surface available for reaction and thereby affecting the observed dissolution behavior. A similar surface-area effect is seen when comparing Mn compacts with Mn flakes, indicating that particle morphology and exposed area influence dissolution kinetics. Regarding intermetallic phases, adding Ti to the aluminum melt changes the iron-containing phase from Al5Fe2 to Al2Fe, but this phase replacement does not affect the dissolution rate. Adding Si substantially inhibits Fe dissolution kinetics. The provided excerpt does not report numerical dissolution rates, kinetic constants, temperatures, dissolution times, or the precise experimental conditions needed to reach complete dissolution. Therefore, those details—including the temperature and time required for Mn or Fe dissolution—must be obtained from other sections of the article. It also does not identify all intermetallic phases formed during dissolution, beyond the Ti-associated Al5Fe2-to-Al2Fe transformation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes dissolution as mass-transfer controlled and models the Mn and Fe flux through a liquid diffusion boundary layer using Fick’s law. After 9 minutes, the calculated fluxes into a 500 g aluminum melt are 3.2 × 10^-3 g/s for Mn and 9.2 × 10^-3 g/s for Fe. Thus, the measured Fe dissolution flux is about 2.9 times the Mn flux, although a simplified calculation based on comparable convection and phase-layer thickness predicts Fe to be 1.4 times higher. The discrepancy is attributed partly to Fe flakes disintegrating into smaller particles and therefore having greater reactive surface area, while compact as-cast Mn flakes mainly react at their surface. The Mn dissolution rate constant is approximately 1.5 × 10^-5 m/s, and stronger stirring increases dissolution: 5-second stirring produced a substantially higher Mn rate than 3-second stirring. Dissolution was studied at approximately 750 °C; the excerpt specifically reports concentrations and microstructures after 9 minutes, rather than a definitive time required for complete dissolution. Dissolution proceeds through intermediate intermetallic phases rather than direct solid dissolution. In the Al-Mn system, Al11Mn4, a lambda-designated phase, and c2 were observed, with Al11Mn4 and lambda having similar thicknesses and c2 somewhat thinner. The excerpt does not identify the Fe intermetallic phases.

Mn dissolution was studied at 750 °C using 90 pct Mn compacts in pure Al and Al–Ti containing 0.12 pct Ti. The Mn dissolution rate was substantially lower in the Al–Ti melt than in pure Al. For Mn in molten Al, intermediate phases form rapidly to a characteristic thickness and then grow slowly as a package penetrates into the Mn particle, with little further increase in layer thickness. Three phases form between Mn and the liquid: c2, Al11Mn4, and λ. The c2 layer is relatively thin and is identified as the principal obstacle to Al diffusion; void formation near the c2/Mn interface indicates a Kirkendall effect, which progressively reduces bonding and inhibits further dissolution. Mn compacts dissolve faster than flakes, likely because particle surface area and shape affect Mn transport; oxide films and reduced convection can locally cause supersaturation and thicker phase growth. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a quantitative dissolution rate or a complete kinetic law for solid titanium dissolving in molten aluminum. It indicates that interaction is strongly temperature- and time-dependent. Wetting improves substantially as temperature rises: contact angles for several commercial aluminum alloys decrease from about 70° at 670°C to 20–30° at 740°C, while brazing experiments commonly use approximately 670–720°C. Intermetallic growth increases with brazing temperature; joints brazed at 710–720°C were weaker than those brazed at 670–680°C. Holding time also affects the interaction: with Al-10Si-1Mg, joint strength initially rises rapidly during the first minute as wetting and oxide removal occur, reaches a maximum after about 25 minutes, and then decreases during prolonged holding because shrinkage cavities and intermetallic layers develop. The reported phases depend on filler composition. Pure aluminum produces the thickest TiAl3 layer, while alloying additions—especially silicon—suppress intermetallic growth. Identified phases include TiAl3, Ti8CuAl23, Al3Ti, CuAl2, Ag2Al, Ti7Al5Si12, Ti8Al23, Al5Si12Ti7, and Al12Si3Ti5. Al-Ni filler forms thinner TiAl2 than the usual TiAl3 layer. Thus, the excerpt supports dissolution/interfacial reaction beginning during molten-Al contact near 670°C and becoming more pronounced at higher temperatures, but it does not specify a direct Ti dissolution temperature or rate.

It does provide related phase-equilibrium and processing information. The authors state that Al3M (including Al3Ti) has a peritectic relationship with the terminal α-Al solid solution, and that under equilibrium solidification the first solid phase is primary/properitectic Al3M. For alloy preparation, they used a monolithic Al3Ti master alloy rather than pure titanium, noting that Al3Ti melts at 1350 °C while pure Ti melts at 1688 °C; this is a melting-point comparison, not a measured Ti-dissolution temperature. The relevant titanium-containing intermetallic is Al3Ti. More generally, Al3M trialuminides initially form as metastable cubic L12 precipitates during decomposition of supersaturated Al-M solid solutions, while their equilibrium structures are tetragonal D022 or D023. The excerpt also discusses Al3Ti precipitation being absent in conventionally solidified dilute Al-Ti alloys during aging, attributed to insufficient supersaturation and the relatively large lattice mismatch, but this concerns solid-state precipitation rather than dissolution in molten aluminium.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames titanium dissolution in molten aluminium as a solid–liquid interaction governed by dissolution kinetics. It distinguishes static experiments, in which the liquid becomes saturated unless solute is removed, from kinetic conditions involving motion of the solid or liquid. The present study is identified as type (2) dissolution in Siller’s classification: direct alloying, involving the formation of surface films or diffusion layers under static, isothermal conditions. Two possible rate-controlling mechanisms are described: diffusion of titanium atoms through a saturated liquid boundary layer, or a slower interfacial chemical step in which solid titanium dissolves into the liquid. The rate may depend on time, temperature, solid-phase alloying elements, liquid-phase metallic additions, surface area/volume ratio, surface preparation, impurities, and physical changes caused by alloying. The passage states that aluminium wets oxide-free titanium and that mechanical cleaning, fluxes, grit blasting, or etching can prepare the surface. It mentions reported Ti–Al phases including a TiAl compound and a newly reported ordered hexagonal Ti3Al phase. One cited X-ray study placed Ti3Al formation at approximately 20–30 wt% aluminium at 1000–1200°C. However, this excerpt does not provide the measured dissolution rate or a definitive temperature at which titanium dissolves; 1000–1200°C refers to reported phase formation, not necessarily the onset of dissolution.

The investigated material is described generally as a Zr/Sc-modified Al-Mg alloy. Sc and Zr additions promote Al3(Sc,Zr) formation, which acts as a heterogeneous nucleation site, refines α-Al grains, improves coherency with the matrix, and increases resistance to coarsening because Zr diffuses more slowly than Sc. The excerpt states that rapid solidification enables extended solubility and solid-solution strengthening; the equilibrium maximum solubilities cited are 0.2 at.% Sc and 0.08 at.% Zr in Al, but these are not recommended LPBF compositions or optimum alloying levels. Heat treatment produced secondary Al3(Sc,Zr) and Mn/Mg-rich phases, yet no Mn concentration is given. The reported process condition—250 W laser power, 833 mm/s scan speed, stripe scanning—yielded 401.4 ± 5.7 MPa tensile strength in the as-built alloy, while aging at 325 °C for 2 h produced 536.0 ± 1.7 MPa strength and 14.8 ± 0.8% elongation. Additional sources are required to answer the composition and optimization question for Er, Sc, Zr, Ce, and Mn comprehensively.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several Al-Ce-based compositions processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). It describes a broader class of near-eutectic aluminum alloys containing approximately 6–16 wt% Ce. Specific examples include an Al-10Ce-8Mn alloy produced by LPBF and the Al-10.5Ce-3.1Ni-1.2Mn alloy studied in detail. The analyzed alloy was measured as 84.92 wt% Al, 10.50 wt% Ce, 3.09 wt% Ni, and 1.18 wt% Mn, with minor Si, Fe, and Mg impurities; its nominal designation is AM Al-Ce-Ni-Mn. Thus, the typical Ce range represented in this excerpt is roughly 6–16 wt%, with about 10–10.5 wt% Ce appearing in the cited LPBF examples. The passage characterizes these as near-eutectic Al-Ce alloys but does not provide the binary Al-Ce eutectic composition, eutectic temperature, or a detailed definition of the Al-Ce eutectic. It also indicates why these compositions are of interest: Ce has low solubility in the Al matrix and helps resist microstructural coarsening and preserve mechanical performance at elevated temperatures. The excerpt therefore supports composition and Ce-content information, but not a precise numerical answer for the Al-Ce eutectic itself.
